title: The Crease in Your Earlobe May Be Warning You About Your Heart. South Asians Should Pay Attention.
excerpt: A diagonal line across the earlobe — known as Frank's sign — has been linked to coronary artery disease for over 50 years. A 2026 diagnostic model says it may be one of the strongest independent predictors of cardiac risk, and the community most vulnerable to heart disease is the least likely to know about it.
body:
Walk into any doctor's office in Mumbai or Chicago and ask about Frank's sign. Most physicians will pause. Some will nod. A surprising number will have no idea what you are talking about.

That is a problem. Because a single diagonal crease running from the tragus to the outer edge of your earlobe — first described by Dr Sanders T. Frank in 1973 — may be one of the cheapest, fastest, and most accessible warning signs for coronary artery disease ever identified. And the community it matters most to is the one least likely to have heard of it.

What the Science Actually Says

Frank noticed the crease in 20 patients presenting with angina. In the five decades since, more than a hundred studies have tested the association. The Copenhagen City Heart Study — a 35-year prospective trial — found that the earlobe crease, along with xanthelasma and crown-top baldness, independently predicted ischemic heart disease and myocardial infarction after adjusting for every traditional risk factor including cholesterol, smoking, diabetes, and blood pressure.

The numbers are hard to ignore. In autopsy studies, bilateral deep earlobe creases predicted pre-existing cardiac disease with 79.5 per cent sensitivity. A coronary arteriography study by Pasternac and Sami found 91.1 per cent positive predictive value. A January 2026 study published in Lipids in Health and Disease by Sun et al. went further, building a diagnostic model combining the earlobe crease with a novel lipid ratio called TyHGB and traditional risk factors. The combined model outperformed any single indicator alone.

The mechanism is not fully understood, but the leading theory is compelling. The earlobe is supplied by end arteries with no collateral circulation. Any process that degrades elastic fibres and weakens microvasculature — the same process that drives coronary atherosclerosis — shows up in the earlobe first, like a canary in a coal mine etched into your skin.

Why South Asians Cannot Afford to Ignore This

South Asians have a three-to-five-fold higher risk of myocardial infarction and cardiovascular death compared to other ethnic groups. This is not driven by lifestyle alone. Genetic predispositions to visceral adiposity, insulin resistance, elevated lipoprotein(a), and smaller, denser LDL particles create a baseline risk that traditional screening tools were not calibrated to catch.

The standard Framingham risk calculator — developed primarily on white American populations — consistently underestimates cardiovascular risk in South Asians. A 45-year-old Indian American man with textbook-normal cholesterol and blood pressure can still have calcified coronary arteries. The community knows this intuitively. Every diaspora family has a story about the uncle who had a heart attack despite being thin and vegetarian.

This is precisely where Frank's sign adds value. It is visible, free, requires no lab work, and is independent of the traditional risk factors that already mislead South Asian screening. A case-control study conducted in Pakistan — the first of its kind in South Asia — confirmed the association between diagonal earlobe crease and coronary artery disease in the region's population.

What You Should Actually Do

Frank's sign is not a diagnosis. It is a signal. Here is how to use it.

Look at your earlobes in a mirror. A diagonal crease that runs at roughly 45 degrees from the tragus to the outer rim of the lobe — especially if it is bilateral, deep, and complete — is what clinicians call a positive Frank's sign. Partial or shallow creases in people over 70 are less specific. But in anyone under 60, a clear bilateral crease deserves attention.

If you see it, do not panic. Do schedule a cardiovascular risk assessment with a doctor who understands South Asian-specific risk. Ask for a coronary artery calcium score — a low-cost CT scan that directly measures plaque in your arteries. Request lipoprotein(a) testing, which most standard lipid panels skip entirely. And share the information with your family, because the genetic architecture that predisposes both the crease and the coronary disease runs in families.

The Bigger Picture

The frustrating irony of Frank's sign is that it has been hiding in plain sight for half a century. It appears in medical textbooks. It has been validated in prospective trials, case-control studies, autopsy series, and now computational diagnostic models. The 2026 study by Sun et al. is not a breakthrough discovery — it is a refinement of something we have known for decades.

Yet it remains largely absent from routine clinical practice, particularly in primary care settings serving diaspora communities. Cardiologists in India are more likely to know about it than family physicians in Fremont or Edison.

For a community that faces the world's highest burden of cardiovascular disease and the least calibrated screening tools, the earlobe crease is not a curiosity. It is a clinical prompt that costs nothing and takes five seconds. The only thing it requires is that someone — a doctor, a family member, or the person looking in the mirror — knows to look.

Sources: Lipids in Health and Disease (2026), Circulation (AHA), Indian Journal of Dermatology, Cureus, Forensic Science, Medicine and Pathology
